items.title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
items.summary: Treasury yields above 5% are raising borrowing costs for households and the federal government, highlighting the challenge of financing $2 trillion deficits.
items.body: Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

items.title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package of 'everyday fixes'
items.summary: The chancellor will axe tariffs on some staples as part of plans to give households "breathing space".
items.body: John Healey will remove import taxes on marmalade, gherkins and more than 100 products in a bid to give families "breathing space" with the cost of living at the Budget . The chancellor on Wednesday will promise a fresh series of "everyday fixes" to ease the pressure on households. The measures will also include an end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent. But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises". Ahead of the Budget, the government said it is removing tariffs on more than 100 "family favourite" products, while supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser costs and households reliant on heating oil.

items.title: Anthropic reveals rapid revenue gains and larger losses in stock market filing
items.summary: Market debut of AI company behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of the AI boom’s financial viability Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US…
items.body: Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom. Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June. “We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.

items.title: What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
items.summary: The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.
items.body: US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week. Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs. The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s. The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets." The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China , rising costs and two conflicts.

items.title: Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened
items.body: In the most recent round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) in the euro area, covering the third quarter of 2026, euro area firms widely reported a further net increase in interest rates on bank loans (net 46%, compared with 42% in the previous quarter). Large firms reported increases more often (net 55%, up from 41%) than small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) (net 38%, down from 43%). At the same time, a net 27% of firms (down from 31% in the previous quarter) reported increases in other financing costs (i.e. charges, fees and commissions) and in collateral requirements (net 14%, up from 10%) (Chart 1). In this survey round, firms reported that the availability of bank loans had declined by more than their needs.

items.title: China’s tax offices issue disclosure orders as offshore asset grace period ends
items.summary: Local tax bureaus across China are continuing to step up oversight following the expiration of the country’s grace period for the reporting of offshore trusts last Thursday, part of an ongoing push to spur voluntary tax disclosures. Municipal tax authorities in Beijing published…
items.body: Local tax bureaus across China are continuing to step up oversight following the expiration of the country’s grace period for the reporting of offshore trusts last Thursday, part of an ongoing push to spur voluntary tax disclosures. Municipal tax authorities in Beijing published notices for 21 individuals on the official website last Thursday – the expiry date of the 90-day grace period – ordering them to submit tax documentation linked to offshore trusts. The notices, issued to “tighten tax collection over offshore trusts”, direct taxpayers to carry out a self-review of any offshore trusts they established or hold an interest in and furnish relevant documents to tax authorities within 15 days in compliance with the law. Earlier this month, tax authorities in Qingdao – a coastal hub in China’s eastern Shandong province – issued a comparable yet more pointed notice to a local taxpayer.

items.title: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone
items.summary: Apple on Monday said it was aware of the issue and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty.
items.body: Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for pre-orders. But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge. Apple on Monday said it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." Apple says on its website that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out-of-warranty.

items.body: Anthropic on Monday unveiled its Form S-1 filing , taking the company one step closer to completing its long-awaited move to the public markets, which is now seen as almost guaranteed to come this year. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi place 95% odds that the artificial intelligence giant officially announces an initial public offering by the end of 2026. Kalshi defines officially announcing an IPO as either the Securities and Exchange Commission declaring an S-1 effective, a priced IPO or an exchange assigning a ticker to a stock. Anthropic is aiming to start trading the week of Nov. 16, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal . Traders on Kalshi place just a 14% chance that the company begins trading before then. On the Polymarket platform, traders give a 69% chance that Anthropic will list on a public exchange and open for trading by Nov. 20.

items.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
items.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
items.body: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US. The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer. Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing. The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

items.body: Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units. Reports of cracks have emerged on Reddit and social media platforms since the handset went on general sale globally on Friday. Experts said there had been too few examples to determine whether there was a more serious problem with Apple’s first foldable device, which retails from $1,999 (£1,499). “We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said. One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it and posted their experience on Reddit .

items.title: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
items.body: Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050. The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate. Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment. COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition. But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity.

items.title: China drafts rules to protect trade secrets from ‘foreign entities’
items.summary: China has drafted special rules to protect the country’s trade secrets and is seeking public feedback on the proposed strictures, the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. In the draft document, the ministry said the rules apply “where a foreign entity engages in acts infringing…
items.body: China has drafted special rules to protect the country’s trade secrets and is seeking public feedback on the proposed strictures, the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. In the draft document, the ministry said the rules apply “where a foreign entity engages in acts infringing upon Chinese trade secrets in the course of international economic, trade and related activities” and those acts endanger or pose a real threat to “China’s national sovereignty, security and development interests”. Under the draft rules, the ministry could impose one or more measures on foreign entities found to have engaged in prohibited conduct, including restricting or banning their trade in goods, technology and services involving China and curbing new investment in China.

items.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push

items.body: Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency. The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people. Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July.

items.body: A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market. A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading. Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500 . That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up. Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle .

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

items.summary: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports Microsoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the…
items.body: Microsoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce. This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally. Some of Microsoft’s most recognizable divisions – including Xbox, Windows and Copilot, its AI tool – will be participating in the offer, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Employees in certain divisions, including in cybersecurity, datacenters and marketing, would not be eligible for the offer, it said.

items.title: Exoskeletons, anyone? China showcases next-gen technology at annual trade fair
items.summary: From drone lasers to lightweight exoskeletons, Chinese manufacturers used the country’s biggest trade fair to showcase a new wave of hi-tech, and sometimes quirky, hardware to global buyers this week. The vast range of next-generation devices – often on offer at surprisingly…
items.body: From drone lasers to lightweight exoskeletons, Chinese manufacturers used the country’s biggest trade fair to showcase a new wave of hi-tech, and sometimes quirky, hardware to global buyers this week. The vast range of next-generation devices – often on offer at surprisingly affordable prices – is the product of a relentless innovation drive under way in China, as firms plough funds into research and development to cope with intense competition at home and rising trade barriers overseas. The R&D wave is helping Chinese exporters expand their global sales even amid an era of higher tariffs. As of Monday last week, a whopping 189,000 buyers from 214 countries and regions had attended the October Canton Fair in Guangzhou, up 13.3 per cent from the previous edition of the trade expo in April.

items.title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
items.summary: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
items.body: Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday. The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made. The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners. Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill. The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.

items.title: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
items.summary: Comey for years has been targeted by President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017.
items.body: Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request. Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it. He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information. The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication." According to a court filing by Comey, who is seeking to dismiss the new case, the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.

items.title: Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
items.summary: The economic is positive now but come January things could become trickier for the Labour government
items.body: The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them. There are codenames. The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media. Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising. As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertà, akin to his fellow Yorkshireman Geoffrey Boycott's at times ultra-defensive stance on a cricket pitch.

items.title: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees
items.summary: Application made for group claim seeking compensation for companies for alleged overcharging on customer card payments Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees. The law…
items.body: Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees. The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020. The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result. The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses.

items.title: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
items.summary: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
items.body: Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was. These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking. They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude. But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world. In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

items.title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
items.summary: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an…
items.body: Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue. Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels. Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue. It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.

The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.

items.summary: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.…
items.body: European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East. Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections. Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.

items.summary: Marcus Perkins, who owns a hair and beauty salon in Brierley Hill, says he is scared for the future.
items.body: After 22 years running a salon, Marcus Perkins says he is increasingly worried about the future of the hair and beauty industry. Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to employ staff and invest in apprenticeships, he says, while more salons are turning to self-employed models to survive. "Seeing salons close on the high street is very scary," he said. "I'm very scared myself. Luckily it hasn't happened yet but who knows what the future holds?" Perkins is among more than 2,000 salon owners who have signed an open letter calling on the Chancellor John Healey to cut VAT on hair and beauty services from 20% to 10% in this week's Budget. The letter is backed by the British Hair Consortium (BHC), which argues rising business costs are placing increasing pressure on traditional salon employers.

items.title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
items.summary: Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions…
items.body: The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia. Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”. Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.

items.title: Elon Musk says more than 200 neoclouds face 'guppy-level death'
items.summary: Investors are already questioning the debt-fueled expansion of neoclouds and whether the large AI infrastructure build-out will generate long-term returns.
items.body: Elon Musk said that more than 200 neocloud companies could collapse, sending shares in those companies whipsawing. Nebius , Iren and CoreWeave all fell in early trading, adding pressure to a sector already facing investor concerns about debt-fueled expansion and whether the large AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns. The stocks all rebounded later in the day. "As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla , said on a post on X on Sunday. "That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many," he added. Musk's SpaceX operates its own data centers through which it sells computing capacity.

items.body: Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said. The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode” . John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”. However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work. “The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation.

items.title: Lula wins Brazil runoff after prediction markets favored Bolsonaro
items.summary: While prediction market odds pointed to a clear Bolsonaro victory, Lula emerged the winner in a tight race.
items.body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected president of Brazil on Sunday in a runoff election, an upset that prediction markets odds failed to anticipate. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro , the right-wing candidate and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, by 51.8% to 48.2%, according to the country's Superior Electoral Court. As late as Sunday afternoon, Lula remained a significant underdog on prediction markets. Even just after 8:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, Lula's odds were at 21% on Kalshi. Bolsonaro's odds on prediction markets surged after first-round voting on Oct. 4, with both Kalshi and Polymarket giving Bolsonaro an over 80% chance of ousting Lula. The Kalshi contract asked, "Brazil Presidential election winner?" and was verified by reporting from the Associated Press. Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour has previously defended Kalshi's election contracts.

items.summary: A wholesale plunder of local communities via casino-gaming took place and racing was content to sit on sidelines Has it really been almost a year since racing’s last bout of Budget-related anxiety? Apparently so, because having successfully persuaded Rachel Reeves to exempt…
items.body: Has it really been almost a year since racing’s last bout of Budget-related anxiety? Apparently so, because having successfully persuaded Rachel Reeves to exempt racing from a (modest) hike in betting duty in 2025, here we are again, nervously anticipating Wednesday’s budget amid warnings that John Healey could effectively sound the death-knell for high-street betting shops. Healey is widely expected to raise the rate of Machine Games Duty (MGD) in the budget, a move which could, according to some predictions, lead the closure of thousands of high-street shops with significant knock-on effects for racing’s income from off-course gambling. The prospect of a significant hike in MGD this week was initially floated by a report from the Social Market Foundation (SMF) thinktank in June.

items.title: Oil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate
items.summary: Investors are worried about the vulnerability of Saudi energy infrastructure and the risk of another disruption to production, refining or export facilities.
items.body: Crude oil prices ticked lower Monday as Saudi Arabia's defense minister held talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran in an effort to ease simmering tensions between the two countries. Brent crude futures lost 91 cents to close at $115.81 a barrel after briefly topping $117 earlier in the session. U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell $1.51 to settle at $101.76. Prices have gained about 12% this month. Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman met Monday with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. Pakistan's Army Chief of Staff Asim Munir and the head of Turkish intelligence Ibrahim Kalin also participated in the talks. Pakistan and Turkey are members of a defense pact with Saudi Arabia. The meeting in Tehran came as Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.

items.title: If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan
items.summary: Andy Burnham has railed against neoliberalism – the historic shift must start with this week’s budget Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister…
items.body: A fter Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country. I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.

items.body: Private equity firms are pouring billions into defense technology as rising military spending and geopolitical tensions fuel an investment boom. Traditional buyout investors are increasingly backing younger, high-growth firms in the sector, according to PitchBook data, with private equity growth investments in defense reaching $4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up from $500 million in 2024. As defense tech companies mature, analysts say private equity, debt and other forms of financing are expected to become more important in bridging the gap between innovation and industrial-scale production, as venture capital alone may not be enough to finance companies' expansion.

items.title: Donald Trump has been a disaster for rural America | Steven Greenhouse
items.summary: The president’s policies have taken such a toll on farmers that Republicans face trouble in deep-red states Donald Trump’s policies have been a disaster for the nation’s farmers, so much so that a near electoral miracle may soon happen: Kansas, one of the deepest red, most rural…
items.body: D onald Trump’s policies have been a disaster for the nation’s farmers, so much so that a near electoral miracle may soon happen: Kansas, one of the deepest red, most rural states, may elect its first Democratic senator in nearly a century . Since Trump won farm country handily in 2024, many rural voters in Kansas, Iowa and elsewhere have soured on him because the price of diesel fuel, a key input for farming, has soared by nearly 70%, because farm bankruptcies have surged and because Trump’s trade wars have significantly reduced agricultural exports. Rural voters are so upset with Trump that polls show that Republican Senate candidates stand a good chance of losing in Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska and Texas, even though Trump won those rural states by 13 percentage points or more in 2024.

items.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
items.summary: Elon Musk said in an X post that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase GPUs.
items.body: SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems. In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses. In a follow-up post , he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027. In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing. The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.

items.title: We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan
items.summary: We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the…
items.body: A t around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare. Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience.

items.title: The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters
items.summary: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not…
items.body: Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained ( Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October ) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question. Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed. Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name.

items.title: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
items.summary: It's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round.
items.body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president, overturning a first-round loss to beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The outcome triggered a sell-off in Brazilian assets as markets were caught off guard. Lula took 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with nearly all ballots counted on Sunday. The results are also historic as it's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round. Brazilian stocks plunged following the unexpected victory, unwinding some of the rally from the first-round result three weeks earlier. That reflected expectations of more market-friendly policymaking by Bolsonaro and broader jitters around Brazil's debt and spending . The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF was 25% lower at 10:30 a.m.

items.title: What the claw arcade game tells us about the cost of living crisis | Zoe Williams
items.summary: No matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenser About a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so I was spending a…
items.body: A bout a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so I was spending a lot more time in arcades. There’s a particular game involving a metal claw – it goes by the name of claw-game. You put in a pound, and try to manipulate the claw to grab a toy that is worth nothing like a pound. You would take that as the price of a bit of family fun, except the claw never grabbed a toy. The frustration for a six-year-old was immense, every lost pound making the probably flammable stuffed hamster more urgently desirable. But it was way worse for me, because I was clinging on to some residual 80s idea of arcade-honour.

items.title: How war, security and coalition math are shaping the Israeli election
items.summary: Israeli voters will head to the polls to cast their votes in a general election on Tuesday.
items.body: Israeli voters will head to the polls Tuesday in an election with implications beyond the country’s borders. It is Israel’s first election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, which killed around 1,200 people and saw more than 250 abducted. The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,500 people . It is also the first vote since the U.S. and Israel began their joint war against Iran in February. Israelis vote for parties rather than directly electing a prime minister, with the Knesset’s 120 seats allocated through proportional representation. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament. Because outright majorities are rare, parties typically form coalitions. The president asks a Knesset member — usually the leader best placed to assemble a 61-seat majority — to form a government.

items.title: Why is Japan tightening its immigration rules?
items.body: TOKYO -- Japan is increasingly becoming dependent on foreign workers, but it has long resisted calling itself an immigrant-receiving country. By the end of 2025, more than 4 million foreign nationals were living in the country. The government has expanded pathways for workers in sectors facing chronic shortages, while also tightening rules for long-term residents and permanent residency. It has capped two major work programs, raised application fees and introduced stricter requirements. That leaves Japan caught between economic need and political pressure to take a tough stance on immigration. What will these changes mean for people hoping to build a life here, and for the businesses and communities that rely on them? To discuss this, Nikkei Asia sat down with Naoko Hashimoto of International Christian University in Tokyo.

items.title: UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’
items.summary: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK…
items.body: Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers. Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand. If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.

items.title: Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work
items.summary: Pilots report pressure to extend working hours and fears of penalties for declaring themselves unfit to fly Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a…
items.body: Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report. The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly. Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead. In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle.

items.body: Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis. The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead. Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed. The chancellor, John Healey , is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country.

items.summary: SoftBank Group reportedly plans to invest $50 billion in Malaysia's technology sector, including artificial intelligence and data centers.
items.body: SoftBank Group plans to make $50 billion of investments in Malaysia, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said, according to a Bloomberg report. Anwar said Saturday that Son had identified locations in Kuching, Sarawak, and peninsular Malaysia for the planned investments following a video conference between the two earlier in the week, the report said . The country's prime minister said the planned investments would focus on artificial intelligence, new technologies and data centers, according to the report. The planned investment comes as Malaysia seeks to become an "AI nation " by 2030, with the government launching a national AI action plan earlier this year to strengthen the country's AI capabilities and infrastructure.

items.title: Sumitomo aims to expand battery energy storage in Japan with UK experience
items.body: TOKYO/LEICESTER, England -- In the leafy outskirts of Leicester, a city in England's East Midlands, an unassuming piece of land houses 30 shipping containers. The long rows of boxes are filled with a combination of batteries and inverters, which have the capacity to store enough energy to power 160,000 homes for two hours.
